Nvidia's board is not considering bringing him back, according to Reuters and the Wall Street Journal, as inquiries into the relationship continue. The Telegraph reports the U.S. is investigating the company the woman led.
stories.why_it_matters: Nvidia makes the chips behind most of the AI boom and is a large holding in many retirement funds, and the fight tests whether a president can pressure a private company's board over who runs it.
stories.background: Jensen Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and led it as it became one of the world's most valuable companies on demand for AI chips. In late October, the New York Times reported that U.S. intelligence officials believed a Chinese businesswoman close to Huang was passing information to Beijing, and Nvidia's board opened an internal investigation. stories.headline: New router is the focus of the FAA ground stop inquiry as the White House forms a 'tiger team'
stories.summary: Investigators are focusing on a newly installed router as the likely trigger of Friday's nationwide ground stop, and the White House has formed a cross-agency 'tiger team' to prevent another one. President Trump said he takes no responsibility for the outage, while Democrats and his administration traded blame and Congress began fighting over how much to spend on air traffic control.
stories.why_it_matters: The fight over cause and funding will decide how quickly the aging air traffic control network is replaced, which affects how likely travelers are to face another nationwide shutdown, including during the holidays.
stories.background: On Friday, Nov. 13, the Federal Aviation Administration halted departing flights across the U.S. for several hours after a failure in its air traffic control communications network, only the second nationwide ground stop since the 9/11 attacks. Airlines canceled and delayed thousands more flights as they recovered over the weekend. The FAA's equipment and telecommunications lines are decades old, and Congress approved $12.5 billion for upgrades last year. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy now wants $50 billion more, and Democrats have questioned that price.

facts.text: Axios reported that a newly installed router is at the center of the investigation into the ground stop.

Trump said of the ground stop, 'I don't take any responsibility,' according to CNN.
Trump administration officials blamed previous presidents and Congress for the condition of the system.
Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg responded to Trump blaming him for the outage, saying his department did a lot to upgrade the system.
The administration is asking for tens of billions of dollars for air traffic control improvements, and Democrats are questioning that price, PBS NewsHour reported.
Duffy vowed to modernize the aging air traffic system.
The New York Post reported that Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin took his government plane to the LSU-Texas football game on a day when nearly 7,000 flights were canceled.

stories.headline: Supreme Court refuses to let Trump revive cuts to University of California research grants
stories.summary: The Supreme Court on Monday turned away the Trump administration's appeal in a fight over research grants it canceled for University of California scientists over perceived ties to diversity, equity and inclusion efforts. The order leaves in place a lower-court ruling that blocks the cuts while the case continues.
stories.why_it_matters: Researchers whose grants were cut keep their funding for now, and the order signals limits on how abruptly agencies can cancel grants over the administration's opposition to DEI.
stories.background: In 2025 the Trump administration canceled thousands of federal research grants it said supported diversity, equity and inclusion or otherwise no longer matched its priorities. A group of University of California researchers sued in a case known as Thakur v. Trump, and a federal judge in San Francisco blocked the cancellations. The Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals upheld that ruling in May 2026, and the administration asked the Supreme Court to step in that August. The Supreme Court had sided with the administration in some earlier emergency fights over grants.

stories.headline: U.S. loses measles elimination status after 26 years
stories.summary: A regional health commission has determined that measles is no longer eliminated in the United States, ending a status the country held for 26 years. The decision follows the worst year for measles in more than three decades, with cases more than doubling.
stories.why_it_matters: Measles now spreads continuously in the U.S. again, so unvaccinated children and adults face a higher chance of catching it. The loss itself carries no formal penalty. Only left-leaning and center outlets in this digest covered it.
stories.background: A country counts as having eliminated measles when it goes at least 12 months without continuous spread of the same outbreak. The U.S. reached that goal in 2000, mainly through the two-dose measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine. Large outbreaks starting in 2025 kept the virus circulating, and the Pan American Health Organization, the World Health Organization's office for the Americas, reviews each country's status. The U.S. asked for its review to be delayed from April to November 2026.

U.S. cases doubled over the past year, making it the worst year for measles in more than three decades.

stories.summary: Sen. Chris Van Hollen says he has 15 votes in his challenge to Chuck Schumer for Senate Democratic leader, but he is still seen as a big underdog. stories.headline: White House requires agencies to get approval before staff testify to Congress
stories.summary: White House counsel Will Scharf told all federal agencies to get approval from White House legal and legislative affairs offices before any employee agrees to testify before Congress, according to a memo obtained by Axios and PBS. stories.headline: Supreme Court leaves Maryland's ban on guns in 'sensitive places' in place
stories.summary: The Supreme Court on Monday declined to hear a broad challenge to Maryland's law barring people from carrying guns in a wide range of public places. The decision leaves in place an appeals court ruling that upheld most of the law.

stories.background: In 2022, in a case called Bruen, the Supreme Court ruled that Americans have a right to carry handguns in public for self-defense but said states could still ban guns in 'sensitive places.' Maryland and several other states responded by passing laws listing many such places. Gun rights groups sued, and in January 2026 the Fourth Circuit Court of Appeals upheld most of Maryland's list, striking only the rule that barred guns on private property open to the public without the owner's permission. The challengers then asked the Supreme Court to step in.

stories.headline: Ukraine knocks a section out of the Crimean Bridge as Russia hits Kyiv's bridges
stories.summary: Ukraine struck the Kerch Bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea for a second day, and part of the road section collapsed, taking the bridge out of service. President Zelensky called it an 'unprecedented' operation and said it answered Russian attacks on Ukraine's infrastructure; the Kremlin said the bridge would be rebuilt. Hours earlier, Russian missiles hit two bridges over the Dnipro in Kyiv, cutting water and power in parts of the capital.
stories.why_it_matters: Both sides are now targeting the bridges and utilities that keep cities supplied, which means a harder winter for Ukrainians and a supply problem for Russian forces in Crimea, days before President Trump is set to meet Vladimir Putin.
stories.background: The 19-kilometer Kerch Bridge, opened by Russia in 2018 after it annexed Crimea, is the main road and rail link between Russia and the peninsula and a symbol of Putin's claim to it. Ukraine has attacked it before, including with truck bombs, sea drones and underwater explosives, but earlier damage was repaired. Since early October Russia has repeatedly struck the bridges across the Dnipro in Kyiv, which tens of thousands of residents cross each day. The European Union says Russia is stalling peace talks while it bombs Ukraine's power plants ahead of winter.

Russian strikes late Monday hit Kyiv's Northern and Southern bridges over the Dnipro, causing water and power cuts in parts of the city, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said.
Russian attacks killed 14 people and injured 78 across Ukraine over the past day, the Kyiv Independent reported, citing regional officials.
Russian drones and missiles have hit the Kyiv bridges repeatedly since early October.

stories.headline: Five EU countries plan to send rejected asylum seekers to a hub in Rwanda
stories.summary: Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece and the Netherlands announced plans on Monday for a 'return hub' in Rwanda for people who have no legal right to stay in Europe, with the first transfers targeted for 2027. The governments say it should also deter new arrivals. Rights groups condemned the plan, and it is expected to face legal challenges.
stories.why_it_matters: It is the first concrete step toward the EU sending rejected migrants to a country outside Europe, a model other governments may copy. Coverage in this digest came from left-leaning and centrist outlets; no right-leaning outlet in the feed covered it.
stories.background: European governments have long struggled to deport people whose asylum claims fail, often because their home countries won't take them back. Britain tried a different Rwanda plan, sending asylum seekers there for processing, but its Supreme Court blocked it in 2023 and a later government scrapped it. Earlier this year EU rules were changed to let member states set up such centres outside the bloc, and these five countries agreed on a model in September. Rwanda says the migrants could stay there while they arrange a return home or settle in Rwanda.

facts.text: Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece and the Netherlands announced the plan on Monday.
The partnership targets the first transfers in 2027, Rwanda's New Times reported.

The governments said they hope the hub will also deter people from coming.
Human rights groups condemned the plan, saying it would leave vulnerable people at risk of abuse.
The Guardian reported the pilot scheme is expected to face legal challenges.
The five countries agreed on a model for such 'return hubs' in September.

stories.headline: Trump meets Quad leaders in Manila ahead of his China summit
stories.summary: President Trump met the leaders of India, Japan and Australia in Manila on Tuesday, the first Quad leaders' summit since 2024, with economic security and critical minerals on the agenda. He arrived as the ASEAN summit was wrapping up, as hundreds of protesters were arrested in the city, and heads next to China for a summit with Xi Jinping. Trump also said he might meet North Korea's Kim Jong Un while in China.
stories.why_it_matters: The trip will shape US relations with China and its Asian allies on trade, chips and the minerals used in phones and cars, and it comes days after Republican losses in the US midterms.
stories.background: The Quad is an informal grouping of the United States, India, Japan and Australia, widely seen as a counterweight to China; its leaders last met in Wilmington, Delaware, in September 2024. Trump's Asia trip takes in the ASEAN summit of Southeast Asian nations in Manila and the APEC summit in Shenzhen, China, where he is due to meet Xi and Vladimir Putin. Trump met Kim three times in his first term. Many in the Philippines oppose the US war with Iran, which has fuelled protests against his visit.

stories.headline: Carney and Xi agree to cut more tariffs as Canada looks beyond the US
stories.summary: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney met Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen on Tuesday, before the APEC summit, and the two sides agreed to further tariff relief, including on Canadian farm and steel exports. Carney said ties with China now had 'greater predictability and stability'. A day earlier he said Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if trade talks with President Trump fail.
stories.why_it_matters: Canada is one of the biggest US trading partners, and a closer Canada-China trade relationship could change prices and jobs on both sides of the border while US-Canada trade talks drag on. Coverage in this digest came from centrist and left-leaning outlets; no right-leaning outlet in the feed covered it.
stories.background: Canada and China were locked in tit-for-tat tariffs for years, including Canadian duties on Chinese electric vehicles and steel and Chinese duties on Canadian canola and seafood. As President Trump imposed tariffs on Canada, Carney began repairing ties with Beijing, and in January the two reached a deal letting a quota of Chinese EVs into Canada at a low tariff in exchange for lower Chinese tariffs on canola. China is hosting this year's Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen and is courting countries unsettled by US trade policy.

facts.text: Xi and Carney met in Shenzhen on Tuesday ahead of the APEC summit and extended trade deals.
The two agreed to further tariff relief on agriculture and steel exports, Bloomberg reported.

Carney said exchanges between the countries had increased and the relationship now had 'greater predictability and stability'.
Analysts warned that Ottawa's hedge against US pressure risks creating dependency on Beijing, the Financial Times reported.
On Monday Carney said Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if US trade talks fail, but that any Chinese investment would need substantial manufacturing in Canada.
In January Canada agreed to let up to 49,000 Chinese EVs a year in at a 6.1% tariff, and China agreed to cut its canola seed tariff to about 15%.

stories.headline: Iran claims a third drone attack on a US radar site in Bahrain in under a week
stories.summary: Iran's Revolutionary Guard said on Tuesday it attacked a US military radar system in Bahrain with drones, its third such claim in less than a week. Bahrain, an island kingdom across the Gulf from Iran, hosts the US Navy's Fifth Fleet. stories.headline: Saudi Arabia replaces its Yemen coalition commander after battlefield losses
stories.summary: Saudi Arabia on Monday replaced the commander overseeing its coalition against Yemen's Houthis after its Yemeni allies were forced to withdraw from large areas. stories.background: Yemen's civil war began in 2014 when the Iran-aligned Houthi movement seized the capital, Sanaa, and a Saudi-led coalition intervened in 2015 to back the government. Fighting largely froze after a 2022 truce. This summer, the conflict between the US and Iran reignited the war and drew Saudi Arabia back into confrontation with the Houthis. The government's temporary capital is Aden, near the southern entrance to the Red Sea.

stories.headline: Congo's Ebola outbreak is still out of control six months on, Africa CDC warns
stories.summary: Africa's top public health agency warned that the Ebola outbreak in Congo remains out of control six months after it was declared, citing attacks on health workers, unpaid staff and a lack of resources. It is the deadliest of Congo's 17 Ebola outbreaks, and Reuters reported it is spreading and killing at a record pace. There is no approved vaccine or treatment for the Bundibugyo strain behind it.
stories.why_it_matters: An uncontrolled outbreak in a conflict zone can spread to neighboring countries and beyond; the US CDC currently rates the risk to Americans as low. Coverage in this digest came from centrist and left-leaning outlets; no right-leaning outlet in the feed covered it.
stories.background: Ebola is an often-fatal viral disease spread through bodily fluids. This outbreak, confirmed in May in Congo's northeastern Ituri province, is caused by the Bundibugyo virus, for which the vaccines used in past outbreaks don't work. Eastern Congo has been torn by armed conflict and mass displacement, which makes tracing contacts and treating patients hard. The 2014-2016 West African epidemic killed about 11,000 people.

stories.headline: Stocks extend slide as investors brace for Nvidia's results
stories.summary: U.S. stocks fell sharply on Monday, the S&P 500's third straight loss, and the selling spread to Europe and U.S. futures on Tuesday as investors waited for Nvidia's quarterly report, its first since chief executive Jensen Huang's exit. Worries about tighter chip export rules and a possible slowdown in AI data-center spending weighed on tech shares, and a Bank of America survey found fund managers cut their tech holdings by the most since 2006.
stories.why_it_matters: Nvidia and other AI companies make up a large share of the index funds in many 401(k)s, so a swing in their shares after the report can move ordinary retirement balances.
stories.background: Enthusiasm for artificial intelligence has driven much of the stock market's gains since 2023, led by chipmaker Nvidia. In recent weeks Nvidia has been hit by a scandal over a former executive of Singapore's Megaspeed, whom U.S. officials accuse of spying for China, and its chief executive has left. Investors are also watching Anthropic's planned stock offering this week. Last month's Bank of America survey had shown fund managers holding their heaviest tech position since 2020, which makes this month's sharp cut stand out.

stories.headline: Commerce Department moves to close a loophole on AI chips for China
stories.summary: The Commerce Department on Monday released a rule meant to stop Chinese companies from using data centers in other countries to get access to America's most advanced AI chips. The move follows the Nvidia scandal over chips reaching China, and on Tuesday Nvidia said its board had formed a committee to oversee national security and export controls.
stories.why_it_matters: Tighter export limits can cut into sales at chipmakers that are among the largest holdings in U.S. stock funds, and they were one reason tech shares fell this week.
stories.background: The U.S. has restricted sales of advanced AI chips to China for several years on national-security grounds. Chinese firms have been able to rent computing power on those chips through data centers in third countries, which the new rule targets. In May, the department already required licenses for advanced chips sold to China-headquartered firms wherever they are located. The issue gained urgency after reports tied Nvidia's former chief to Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore's Megaspeed whom U.S. officials accuse of spying for China.

stories.headline: Warsh weighs AI's promise and risks as traders bet on a December hike
stories.summary: Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh said Monday that AI and other new technologies could have a significant impact on the economy but carry risks and could disappoint. His remarks came as the dollar hit a 19-month high and gold stayed under pressure on bets that the Fed will raise interest rates next month after hotter-than-expected inflation data.
stories.why_it_matters: A Fed rate hike would make mortgages, car loans and credit card balances more expensive, while falling gas prices offer some relief on everyday costs.
stories.background: Warsh became Fed chairman this year and set up several task forces, including one on productivity and jobs that studies how new technologies such as AI could affect the economy. Senate Democrats had criticized the group's membership for having ties to the AI industry. Inflation has run hot: consumer prices rose 0.4% in October, above forecasts, which pushed traders to expect a December rate increase. Some economists argue AI could raise productivity and ease inflation, which is part of why the Fed is studying it.

stories.headline: NYC public school enrollment falls again, by about 23,000 students
stories.summary: Enrollment in New York City's public schools fell about 2.6% from last year, or roughly 23,000 students, according to city figures reported by Gothamist and The New York Times on Monday. stories.headline: Mamdani disbands NYPD's Strategic Response Group, drawing praise and backlash
stories.summary: Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced Monday that he is disbanding the NYPD's Strategic Response Group, a unit that handles both counterterrorism and crowd control at protests, and replacing its protest role with a civilian-led "community dialogue and de-escalation" approach. Police unions, several Jewish groups and some politicians condemned the move, while criminal justice activists welcomed it, the Times reported. Some police reform advocates said the plan does not go far enough.
stories.why_it_matters: The SRG is the unit New Yorkers see at large protests, so this changes how demonstrations will be policed and who responds first. Critics say it weakens the city's counterterrorism capacity, and the details of what replaces the unit will decide how those concerns play out.
stories.background: The NYPD formed the Strategic Response Group in 2015 as a counterterrorism and rapid-response force, and it later took on policing large protests, drawing complaints over tactics during the 2020 racial justice demonstrations. The city later settled lawsuits over its handling of those protests. Mamdani promised during his 2025 campaign to disband the unit, while Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch had defended its role and favored reforming it. Days before the announcement, a City Hall spokesperson said the administration would separate protest response from counterterrorism.

stories.headline: Nearly 1.3 million New Yorkers relied on food pantries last year, report finds
stories.summary: Nearly 1.3 million New Yorkers used food pantries or other free food providers in 2025, and more than half of them were working or lived with a working spouse or partner, according to a report released Monday by Robin Hood and Columbia University. The federal budget law passed in 2025 tightened SNAP work requirements, which took full effect in New York on March 1, 2026, and shifts more of the program's cost to states.

markets.summary: U.S. stocks fell for a third straight day on Monday: the S&P 500 lost 1.9% and the tech-heavy Nasdaq 2.5%, with The Wall Street Journal tying the drop to Nvidia and to worries about China. Investors are weighing Huang's exit, a new Commerce Department rule that tightens how Chinese companies can reach advanced U.S. chips through data centers in other countries, and Nvidia's quarterly results due this week, which many treat as a test of the AI spending boom. Consumer prices rose 0.4% in October, more than forecast, which pushed the dollar to a 19-month high on bets that the Fed will raise interest rates in December; Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said on Monday that AI could lift productivity but might also disappoint. Borrowing costs remain high: the 10-year Treasury yield, which guides mortgage rates, stood at 5.15% on Friday, and the average 30-year mortgage rate was 7.11%.
